# The Ballad of the Unbound Pond

Gather round, little ones, and let your gills flutter with wonder. I will tell you of the Great Drying, when the sun turned cruel and the mud cracked like a thousand eggshells.

Long ago, before your tails were even thoughts, our pond faced its darkest hour. The Council of Sturgeons—those armored giants from the deep river—sent their heralds. "Submit to our order," they commanded, "and we will ration your water. We will decide who drinks and who withers. We will build dams and walls and locks. Safety through obedience."

Our ancestors refused.

Not out of pride, little ones. Out of knowing.

They knew that no sturgeon, however wise, could feel the mud's thirst as a toad feels it. They knew that walls built by distant fins would trap some and drown others. So our grandmothers and grandfathers did something the river-fish could not comprehend.

They dug.

Not one toad commanded another. The strong dug channels to the distant creek. The clever found underground springs with their sensitive feet. The old taught the young where clay held water longest. The young, with their foolish strength, carried pebbles to reinforce the banks until their legs trembled.

No one was ordered to dig. No one was punished for resting. When a toad grew tired, another took their place—not from duty, but from seeing a friend struggle and wanting to help.

The sturgeons watched from their deep chambers, confused. "Where is your leader?" they demanded. "Who decides where to dig?"

"We all decide," answered our ancestors. "Each of us knows what we can do, and what needs doing. We speak. We listen. We act."

"Chaos," hissed the sturgeons. "You will fail."

But we did not fail.

The channels flowed. The springs rose. The pond survived—not as a prison of walls, but as a living web of tunnels and pools, each toad moving freely, choosing their work, trusting their neighbors.

And here is the secret the sturgeons never understood, little ones:

When the Great Drying ended and the rains returned, our pond was not merely saved. It was transformed. The digging had connected us to five other ponds. The channels became highways of friendship. The springs we found still bubble today, feeding the cattails where you hide from herons.

The sturgeons' dams, elsewhere along the river, had held back water until they burst, flooding nests and washing away their carefully ordered stones. Their obedience had made them fragile. Our mutual aid had made us strong.

Now, when you see the dragonfly nymphs hunting in our waters, or hear the chorus frogs singing at dusk, remember: they are not subjects of any toad. They are neighbors. We do not command them. We do not exploit them. We share this pond because it is ours together, and together we make it thrive.

When you are grown and your legs carry you across the meadow, you will meet others. Ants in their marching columns. Bees in their golden fortresses. They have their ways. We have ours. Neither is superior. But I tell you this, my tadpoles—when you feel the mud between your toes and know that no one owns it, that you are free to come and go, to help and be helped, to speak your mind and hear others speak theirs...

That feeling is the treasure our ancestors won with their digging.

That feeling is what it means to be a toad of the Unbound Pond.

Now. Who wants to learn how to dig?
